prime.problem: Every card in this course ends where its evidence ends: a simulation with illustrative inputs, or a single negative control from the posts. Without a list of what is still unmeasured, it's easy to repeat a study that exists or skip a cheap one that doesn't.
prime.fits: The last card of course 1, after the three concept cards. It turns their limits into research questions and marks the ones that feed the capstone paper on false success claims.
expect: ranking by novelty × cheapness × change in practice
prime.goal: Pick one question, say what is already known with a citation, and write a smallest experiment you could run this week.

attend: Why does the compaction question rank above the far cheaper replay-safety question?
Which papers make the per-link question only partly studied, and what exactly do they leave out?
What failure could an evidence contract invite in a coding harness that it couldn't on fixed traces?
Which questions use the done-chain checker as their measuring instrument?

must: Card numbers come from simulations or single negative controls → they show a failure can happen, not how often → most "how often, in which harness, at which link" questions are still open
Related work is run-level, or uses fixed traces and research scaffolds → per-link rates in production coding harnesses are untested → that gap is where the capstone sits

Hold the model and the task fixed and change one harness setting → any difference is attributable to that setting → cheap questions (compaction on or off, one busy policy) can still give causal answers
reference: the arXiv ids and paper names

compress.prompt: Card closed. List the three capstone questions with their status and the paper that makes each open or partly studied. Then write one smallest experiment from memory.
checklist: compaction → false claims: open, one case study with no run counts (2607.13071)
per-link breakage in CLIs: partly studied, OverclaimBench is run-level and file-review only
evidence contract: partly studied, 22.8% → 0.8% on fixed traces, untested in a coding harness
a smallest experiment holds model and task fixed and varies one setting

retrieve.q: Explain why "open" on this card doesn't mean "no study exists", and what it does mean.
answer: it means the writers and the novelty check found none
searches miss work, and new papers appear monthly
so check again before claiming novelty, as the writer flagged for 2609.20211

retrieve.q: Walk through question 2's smallest experiment: what you re-run, what you hash, and what result would change how approvals are recorded.
answer: re-run only the edit step from one recorded state, many times
hash each resulting diff and count distinct hashes
more than one hash means a replayed step can differ from the approved diff
then the approval record must name the diff's sha, so a changed diff invalidates it

retrieve.q: You have $200 and a week. Choose between the per-link CLI study and the crash-injection rig, and defend the choice with the ranking's three factors.
answer: the per-link study fits the $100–500 estimate; the rig is about a week of build
the per-link study feeds the capstone and changes where harness builders put checks
the rig is novel for agents but answers a narrower question (duplicates)
either is defensible if you say which factor you weighted

compare.q: The done-chain card's two field cases are negative controls; question 3 asks for rates. What does a negative control prove that a rate can't, and the other way round?
answer: a negative control proves the links can disagree, with a mechanism you can see
it says nothing about how often
a rate says how often and where, per harness and link
but a rate needs a validated checker, and the control is what shows the checker works

compare.q: That card's simulation gives 1.70 duplicate effects per run under restart; question 7 asks for the real number. Which assumption of the simulation would a crash-injection study test first?
answer: the simulation always crashes in the gap after the effect and before the record
its crash rate of 0.2 is illustrative
a real harness may record before acting, retry inside a call, or dedupe downstream
so the real count could be far lower or higher; only injection tells

predict.q: Question 4's rule: the final message must quote the last test command and its exit code. In a coding harness, predict whether false claims fall, and what else you would see in the diffs if the agent games the rule.
predict.answer: Nobody has measured it; that is why it's open. On fixed traces the evidence contract cut false success from 22.8% to 0.8%, so a fall is plausible. But a harness agent can make the exit code 0 by editing the tests, so watch for a rising share of diffs that touch test files. That is the failure moving to link 4, which is why the experiment counts both.

apply.task: Use the three moves in "How to generate your own" on a harness you've built: split one overloaded status word, write the question the split opens, and design a smallest experiment that changes one setting.
apply.done: You have one word split into at least two recorded states, one question with a status (open, partly studied, done or unknown) and a citation or "unknown", and an experiment that fixes the model and tasks and varies one setting.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: whether an evidence contract would hold up in a real harness?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why run-level studies leave the per-link question open?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: compaction → status inflation, or status inflation → false claim?
Which question would you actually run first, and what would its result change in your own harness?
